questions.q: What is the relationship between df.filter() and df.where() in PySpark?
options: filter() removes columns, where() removes rows
They're genuinely interchangeable — where() exists as a SQL-flavored alias for filter()
where() is deprecated and should never be used
filter() only works on numbers, where() only works on strings
questions.explain: where() exists purely so SQL-background readers feel at home, since WHERE does the same job in Spark SQL (Lesson 59).

questions.q: Why does trips.filter("trip_distance" > 10) silently do the wrong thing?
options: It raises a clear error immediately
It works correctly and is the recommended syntax
It compares the Python string "trip_distance" to the integer 10 using Python's own rules, with no connection to the actual DataFrame column
It filters every row in the DataFrame regardless of the condition
questions.explain: This is a real trap — col() is what actually builds a Spark condition that gets evaluated against the DataFrame's rows.

questions.q: Why must you use & and | instead of Python's and/or when combining filter conditions?
options: & and | only work when there's exactly one condition
Python's and/or are faster, so Spark forbids them by convention only
Spark's Column objects overload the bitwise operators (& and |) for this purpose — and/or don't work the same way on them
There's no real difference between the two forms
questions.explain: This is why each individual condition also needs its own parentheses, due to Python's operator precedence rules.

questions.q: What is the Pandas equivalent of trips.filter(col("trip_distance") > 10)?
options: There is no equivalent operation in Pandas
df[df["trip_distance"] > 10], the boolean indexing pattern from Lesson 24
df.drop("trip_distance")
df.sort_values("trip_distance")
questions.explain: Same underlying concept — keep rows where a condition is true — just a method call instead of bracket indexing.

questions.q: Why do you need col() rather than a plain string when writing a filter condition?
options: col() builds an actual Spark condition object that can be evaluated against every row, rather than a plain Python comparison
col() is only needed for numeric columns, never for text columns
Plain strings work exactly the same as col() in every case
Filter conditions never need col() in PySpark
questions.explain: Without col(), a comparison like "trip_distance" > 10 just evaluates in plain Python, disconnected from the DataFrame.
